newsitem.title: CHINA: Shanghai people indifferent on Hong Kong handover.
newsitem.headline: Shanghai people indifferent on Hong Kong handover.

text.p: While the propaganda machine in Shanghai works overtime pumping out material on the Hong Kong handover, the main reaction to the historic event from residents of China's biggest city so far seems to be indifference.

Pushed for an opinion on China's takeover of the British colony at midnight on June 30, they leaned towards pessimism, sometimes harking back to Shanghai's own experience of being taken over by the communists in 1949.
"It's got nothing to do with me," said one young hotel worker. "I'm numb to it all."
"It doesn't make a difference to me, I just hope Hong Kong doesn't change as a result," said a college student.
"From a national perspective, it's significant, but we prefer to bother about things that have some concrete significance," said a middle-aged taxi driver.
He said he felt the promises by the Chinese government to Hong Kong of "one country, two systems" and "no change for 50 years" were empty and temporary at best.

"It's just a tactic. When the communists came to Shanghai, they said nice things to the capitalists because they wanted to use them, but they got rid of them all in 1958," he said. "This (Hong Kong) is the same."
These sentiments were echoed with more ferocity by another resident.
"It would be better to leave it alone. These people can't even run China properly, how can they handle a place like Hong Kong?" he said.
"Leave it with the British, I say. Anyway, it doesn't affect me one way or the other. I can't go to Hong Kong now, and I won't be allowed to go after, so what's the difference?" he said.
A man recently laid off from a state factory job echoed that view.

"I don't think it's a good thing, actually," he said of the Hong Kong handover. "The political systems are too different, the Communist Party is sure to make a mess of it. They are so corrupt. They say 50 years no change, don't they? It will change long before that."
A local stock broker took a more cautious view.
"It's hard to say what will happen," he said. "It all depends on how much they (the Chinese authorities) interfere in Hong Kong. Let's wait a couple of years to see how they do."
